title: Expelled
hook: England expels its Jews, the start of a long line of expulsions

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blood libels: a lie from Norwich that kept traveling. Your line was lies kill. Did a rumor stop with you? Today a new week begins, in the same country, with an order from the king. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

In the middle of London there is a street called Old Jewry. People walk down it to work every day, past banks and offices. The name is older than any of the buildings. It marks where a Jewish neighborhood once stood: homes, a synagogue, a place where children learned their letters. Then one summer a royal order went out across England, and by the autumn those homes were empty. Today, one word for what happened to them.
screen: `A LONDON STREET CALLED OLD JEWRY.` → `A ROYAL ORDER.` → `EMPTY HOMES BY AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: The king was Edward the First. His order told every Jew in England to leave the kingdom by the feast of All Saints, and said that any who stayed after that would face death. They could take money and goods they could carry. Their houses, their debts owed to them and their synagogues passed to the crown. Some families crossed to France and other lands. Some, tradition says, did not survive the crossing. The order came at the end of a long squeeze. English Jews had been taxed again and again by the crown, restricted in the work they could do, and hit by the false stories we heard yesterday. By the time of the order, the community was far poorer than it had been. Expelled is a hard word. It doesn't mean moved, or migrated. It means pushed out, with a deadline, by people with the power to enforce it. And England's order was not the last. Other kingdoms and cities would issue their own over the following centuries, and in the coming days we will meet some of them. The Torah knows the experience from the inside. Its story keeps returning to leaving: Abraham told to go from his father's house, a people walking out of Egypt. And it turns that memory into a rule about others. In Exodus: "a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." A people that remembers being pushed out is asked to remember it every time someone else arrives at the door.
screen: `EDWARD THE FIRST'S ORDER.` · `LEAVE BY ALL SAINTS.` · `A LONG SQUEEZE BEFORE.` · then, large: `YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of those forced to leave home. Sit still and let your breath slow. Picture your own front door, and everything behind it you'd want to take. Now imagine being told you have a few months, and only what you can carry. Let that settle for a moment. Then widen the picture to the people, then and now, who have stood at that door for real. Hold them in mind, without needing to say anything. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Expelled. Pushed out of a country by order, with a deadline: the fate of England's Jews under Edward the First, and of other communities after them. Today's word.
Your line: pushed out, with a deadline. Today, look up the story of one place near you whose name remembers people who are no longer there. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Jews remember past expulsions in study, in memorial prayers and on fast days such as Tisha B'Av, and some Jewish communities support refugees in memory of their own history.

trapdoor: what you thought: expelled is a dramatic word for moving away.
what it means: it means being pushed out of a country by order, with a deadline, as the Jews of England were under Edward the First.
what a scholar hears: the order came after years of heavy royal taxation; the Torah's answer to such memory is 'ye know the heart of a stranger' (Exodus 23:9).
